newsitem.title: CHINA: HK labour movement plans fight for lost rights.
newsitem.headline: HK labour movement plans fight for lost rights.

text.p: Hong Kong's new government has dealt a blow to the labour movement by striking down key laws on workers' rights, but unions plan to fight at home and abroad to restore the legislation.
Hong Kong's China-appointed parliament passed a government bill late on Wednesday suspending a clutch of labour rights laws pending a review and fresh legislation.
The laws were enacted in the week before Beijing took back the territory on July 1 after 156 years of British colony.

Lee Cheuk-yan, leader of the pro-democracy Confederation of Trade Unions and a former legislator, told Reuters that the unions would turn to international labour bodies for support and would seek legal advice on constitutional aspects.
"The most important laws -- the rights of trade unions to free association and collective bargaining -- were suspended. These laws were the real target...and they succeeded," he said.
"It shows Hong Kong business rules Hong Kong," Lee said, a play on China's policy that "Hong Kong people rule Hong Kong" after the sovereignty change.
Eden Woon, director of the General Chamber of Commerce, applauded the vote and said his chamber would work closely with officials, legislators and employers to work out new laws.
Lee said the unions would continue their drive for the right to collective bargaining on wages and benefits, and for the right to use union funds for political activities.
They would complain to the International Labour Organisation in Geneva on "the violation of freedom of association and collective bargaining set out in international conventions".
Hong Kong subscribes to international covenants on human rights and labour -- the territory's new constitution, the Basic Law, promulgated by China, enshrines those rights.
Legal experts say the legislature's latest move might spark a constitutional conflict because it removed rights already entrenched in law and guaranteed in the constitution.
Lee said the union's lawyers were studying whether the interim parliament had also exceeded its role.
China-controlled handover bodies have said the assembly's role is to pass the minimum of laws needed for the smooth running of the new government until elections next year.
Underlying the labour battle is the deeper issue of Hong Kong's colonial-era elected Legislative Council, which China dissolved and replaced with the present appointed body.
Activists see the government move as an assault on democracy that could lead to a broader attack on existing laws. The legislature is dominated by a powerful pro-China business lobby.
The labour issue is one of several disputes entangling post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, his government and the unelected chamber.
The other quarrels are over his plan to toughen sedition laws, his bill to deport child illegal immigrants and an election law blueprint that would hamper pro-democracy forces.
On Thursday, a newspaper said Tung would also soon unveil guidelines on "national security" that has been used to justify his recent curbs on freedom of association and assembly.
Tung's government argued that the labour laws would blunt Hong Kong's competitive edge.

The freeze drew angry opposition from a tiny minority of legislators. "This administration attempts to undo all the lawful decisions that a former body decided. What message are we sending to the public? What confidence are we issuing to the public?" legislator Leong Che-hung asked within the chamber.
"I object to the way the administration attempts to pressurise this provisional legislature to pass bills in haste for the government's own administrative expedience."
